successors.name: Yayoi Period
successors.text: Kyushu, Shikoku and Honshu south of northern Tohoku, where the Yayoi began "between 500 and 300 BC"

successors.name: Epi Jomon
successors.text: "Hokkaido and Northern Tohōku", where the Jōmon were succeeded by "the related people of the Zoku-Jomon"

ledger.x: 6000 BCE: the Jōmon hunter-gatherers hold the Japanese archipelago in the Initial Jōmon ("Initial (8,500-5,000 BC)"; the period began c.
5000 BCE: the Early Jōmon begins: "Early (5,000-3,520 BC)"; "The Early Jōmon period saw an explosion in population".
3520 BCE: the Middle Jōmon begins: "Middle (3,520-2,470 BC)"; the Sannai Maruyama settlement in Aomori is at its height (Sannai Maruyama page: occupied "(3900 - 2200 BCE)").
2470 BCE: the Late Jōmon begins: "Late (2,470-1,250 BC)".
1250 BCE: the Final Jōmon begins: "Final (1,250-500 BC)"; after 1500 BCE "populations seem to have contracted dramatically".
300 BCE: in Hokkaido and northern Tohoku the Jōmon give way to the related Zoku-Jōmon (Epi-Jōmon), not to the Yayoi.

300 BCE: the Jōmon period ends in the south and centre ("Recent findings have refined the final phase of the Jōmon period to 300 BC") and the Yayoi culture takes Kyushu, Shikoku and Honshu ("Yayoi (c.

certainty.note: No border is recorded; the archipelago's coast is the edge and the inner divisions are cultural, not political.
